articles.title: Leuprorelin Acetate for Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy: A Systematic Review of Clinical Efficacy, Long-Term Outcomes, and Safety Considerations.
articles.abstract: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA; Kennedy disease) is a rare X-linked neuromuscular disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene. Leuprorelin acetate, a luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone agonist, suppresses androgen signaling and is approved for SBMA-associated dysphagia in Japan; however, evidence regarding efficacy remains heterogeneous. PubMed and Embase were searched from inception through June 18, 2026, for studies evaluating leuprorelin in genetically confirmed SBMA. Randomized trials, observational cohorts, natural history-controlled studies, extension studies, and safety case reports were included, and findings were synthesized narratively because of substantial heterogeneity. Eleven studies met inclusion criteria, including eight efficacy studies (460 patients) and three safety-focused case reports. Leuprorelin reduced pathogenic androgen receptor accumulation and improved biochemical markers, including serum creatine kinase and creatinine decline. Although neither pivotal randomized trial demonstrated significant short-term functional improvement at 48 weeks, longer-term studies showed slower decline in Revised Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R), Limb Norris, and Norris Bulbar scores and improved event-free survival from pneumonia and death. Benefits were greatest with earlier treatment, particularly disease duration < 10 years. Leuprorelin was generally well tolerated; common adverse effects included hot flushes, sexual dysfunction, and decreased bone mineral density. Leuprorelin may slow long-term functional deterioration in SBMA, with greater benefit following early initiation and prolonged treatment.

articles.title: The calibration-to-accuracy mapping in P300 spellers does not transport across cohorts and was not restored by tested alignment or local recalibration.
articles.abstract: Objective. A calibration-derived score has been related to online P300-speller accuracy in the same session, always within the cohort measured. We evaluated whether a mapping from that score to expected accuracy transports to withheld cohorts. Approach. Retrospective secondary analysis of BigP3BCI 1.0.0, the largest evaluation of this relationship to date: 18 of 20 studies contributed 271 participants, 739 session-condition records, and 19 611 character selections. The predictor was a decoder's cross-validated discriminability on calibration epochs, one study withheld from development. Between-cohort variation was summarised by the random-effects standard deviation tau. Main results. The association was positive in all 18 cohorts but varied widely ( r 0.190-0.928; participant-level r = 0.714, p < 0.001), with 12 CIs excluding zero. Pooled estimation error was 0.098 (95% CI 0.091-0.107) against a benchmark of 0.146. Calibration did not transport: intercept tau 0.87 (unrepresented-cohort interval -1.97 to 1.85, log-odds); cohort-specific slopes varied more than tenfold (tau 0.43, interval 0.111-2.005). Neither alignment (signal- or score-space) nor either nonlinear boundary meaningfully reduced this heterogeneity. Local recalibration with up to 16 participants did not reliably improve on transporting; refitting both intercept and slope was significantly worse than transporting at the smallest sizes. Median time per selection, a stopping-rule proxy, accounted for 66% of between-cohort slope variance in meta-regression. The four amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cohorts gave an uncorrected slope spread of 0.223, against 0.560 overall. Significance. The evaluated score is a classifier's cross-validated discriminability on each session's calibration data rather than the source studies' undocumented online decoder. That score reproducibly signals within-session accuracy, but its mapping to accuracy is cohort-specific and supports ranking sessions after local validation rather than reporting accuracy elsewhere. The four-cohort ALS subgroup appeared more homogeneous than the full archive, illustrating how conclusions about transportability from a small cohort set can be fragile.

articles.title: The decline of respiratory function in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients and the role of non-invasive ventilation.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease characterized by a poor prognosis, with an average survival of 3 to 5 years from symptom onset. Respiratory failure is the main cause of death, and non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is a cornerstone in the management of ALS patients. This single-center retrospective study was conducted at Siena University Hospital between 2010 and 2024 to analyze respiratory function parameters in ALS patients undergoing NIV, stratified by disease severity and followed over one year, to assess the relationship between lung function decline and the timing of NIV initiation. A total of 49 patients (29 males, 20 females; mean age 67±12 years) were enrolled, and 31 (63%) received NIV. Clinical and functional parameters, including forced vital capacity (FVC), pCO₂, respiratory symptoms at baseline, and longitudinal measurements of sitting FVC (FVCsit%), supine FVC (FVCsup%), and pCO₂, were collected and analyzed over time. Differences in FVC decline were observed according to the timing of NIV initiation. Among non-severe patients, those starting NIV at T0 showed a 22.5% reduction in FVC over a mean follow-up of 12.8±4.8 months. Patients initiating NIV at T2 exhibited a reported FVCsit decline of 26% (p=0.0488) and a survival of 51.3±50 months from NIV initiation, whereas those starting later (T3-T6) showed a greater decline (FVCsit decline 34%, p=0.0002) and shorter survival duration (15.7±28.6 months). These findings describe differences in respiratory function trajectories and observed survival among patients initiating NIV at different follow-up time points. However, the retrospective design, small sample size, baseline differences between groups, and potential confounding and survival-related selection bias limit causal interpretation. Further studies are needed to clarify the relationship between NIV initiation timing and clinical outcomes in ALS.

articles.title: Advances in plant polysaccharide research for neurodegenerative diseases therapy.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and multiple sclerosis (MS), represent a growing global public health burden with limited therapeutic options. Plant polysaccharides are natural, biocompatible, and multi-target bioactive macromolecules that have emerged as promising candidates for ND intervention. This review systematically summarizes recent progress in elucidating the structural characteristics, structure-activity relationships, and neuroprotective mechanisms of plant polysaccharides. Key structural features such as molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, glycosidic bond configuration, and spatial conformation critically modulate the biological activity of these molecules. Furthermore, we summarize the numerous protective effects of plant polysaccharides against NDs, including inhibiting abnormal protein aggregation, alleviating oxidative stress via the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway, suppressing neuroinflammation through the NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways, regulating neuronal apoptosis, and modulating the gut-brain axis. Clinical translation challenges, primarily blood-brain barrier penetration, structural heterogeneity, and insufficient clinical validation, are discussed. Future directions include developing advanced delivery systems, conducting large-scale randomized controlled trials, and exploring synergistic combination therapies. Collectively, plant polysaccharides show considerable promise as potential multi-target candidates for the intervention of NDs, although further studies are needed to clarify their therapeutic potential and facilitate clinical translation.

articles.title: Brain clearance of protein aggregates in degenerative diseases: the role of microglia and astrocytes.
articles.abstract: Protein aggregation and impaired clearance constitute central pathological hallmarks of numerous neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and frontotemporal dementia. Misfolded proteins, both extracellular and intracellular, disrupt proteostasis and contribute to synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and neuronal loss. Within the central nervous system, glial cells serve as the primary mediators of pathological protein clearance. Microglia detect, phagocytose, and degrade aggregated proteins. However, under chronic pathological stress, microglial function turns from clearing pathological proteins to paradoxically facilitating their spread. Astrocytes, which provide metabolic and homeostatic support for neurons, also participate in the clearance of aggregates through phagocytosis and glymphatic drainage. Critically, crosstalk between astrocytes and microglia enhances the clearance: microglia can recruit and process aggregates internalized by astrocytes, while astrocyte-derived signals modulate the microglial phagocytic activity. Aging, genetic risk factors, or sustained neuroinflammation may reduce the efficiency of glial removal of aggregates and accelerate disease progression. Understanding the cellular and molecular underpinnings of microglial and astrocytic clearance pathways is essential for developing therapies aimed at restoring proteostasis and mitigating neurodegeneration.

articles.title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a CHCHD10 R15L family.
articles.abstract: Familial forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are potential candidates for gene-directed therapies, but many recently identified genes remain poorly characterized. Here, we provide a comprehensive clinical, neuropathological and biochemical description of familial ALS (fALS) caused by the heterozygous p.R15L missense mutation in the gene CHCHD10. Using a cross-sectional study design, we evaluated five affected and nine unaffected individuals from a large seven-generation pedigree with at least 68 affected members. The pedigree suggests a high (68%-81%) but incomplete disease penetrance. Through cloning of the disease allele from distant members of the family, we establish the disease haplotype in the family. Notably, the haplotype was distinct from that of a previously reported p.R15L mutation carrier with ALS, demonstrating that the variant is in a mutational hotspot. The clinical presentation was notable for being highly stereotyped; all affected individuals presented with the rare ALS variant flail arm syndrome (FAS; also known as brachial amyotrophic diplegia or Vulpian-Bernhardt syndrome), suggesting greater involvement of the cervical spinal cord. Consistently, neuropathology from one family member demonstrated substantially increased CHCHD10 protein aggregation and neuronal loss (though absent TDP-43 pathology) in the cervical versus lumbar spinal cord. This FAS phenotype could be captured by a simple timed finger-tapping task, suggesting potential utility for this task as a clinical biomarker. Additionally, through analysis of fibroblast lines from 12 mutation carriers, isogenic induced pluripotent stem cells and a knock-in mouse model, we determined that CHCHD10 with the R15L variant is stably expressed and retains substantial function both in cultured cells and in vivo, in contrast to prior reports. Conversely, we find loss-of-function (LoF) variants are more common in the population but are not associated with a highly penetrant form of ALS in the UK Biobank (31 in controls; 0 in cases). Together, this argues against LoF and in favour of toxic gain-of-function as the mechanism of disease pathogenesis, similar to the myopathy-causing variants in CHCHD10 (p.G58R and p.S59L). Finally, through proteomic analysis of CSF of variant carriers, we identify that CHCHD10 protein levels are elevated approximately 4-fold in mutation carriers, and that affected and unaffected individuals are differentiated by elevation of two neurofilaments: neurofilament light chain (NfL) and peripherin (PRPH). Collectively, our findings help set the stage for gene-directed therapy for a devasting form of fALS, by establishing the likely disease mechanism and identifying clinical and fluid biomarkers for target engagement and treatment response.

articles.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.title: Current findings, application, and diagnosis of magnetic resonance imaging in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder within the motor neuron disease (MND) spectrum, characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. The clinical phenotype ranges from pure motor syndromes to forms with cognitive and behavioral impairment, and the pathological burden extends beyond the motor system. Diagnosis remains primarily clinical, supported by electrophysiology and exclusion of mimics. Therefore, objective imaging biomarkers are urgently needed. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is widely used as an auxiliary and differential diagnostic tool in ALS. T1- and T2-weighted imaging can assess cortical thickness, gray matter atrophy, and signal changes. Diffusion tensor imaging probes white matter microstructure. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy detects neurochemical alterations. Resting-state functional MRI assesses functional connectivity and network organization. Susceptibility-weighted imaging is sensitive to iron and calcium deposition. Ultra-high-field MRI provides higher resolution and improved metabolite quantification. This critical review summarizes current findings on MRI in ALS, but importantly organizes the evidence by the specific question being addressed: pathological/histological correlates, diagnostic or discriminatory performance, and clinical associations with phenotype, severity, progression, and prognosis. We also discuss major limitations, including methodological heterogeneity, limited standardization, small and clinically heterogeneous cohorts, frequent use of healthy rather than disease controls, and scarce multicenter validation. Although advanced MRI has revealed robust group-level alterations, none of these techniques has yet become established in routine clinical diagnosis of ALS. We, therefore, distinguish promising research findings from validated clinical biomarkers and outline priorities for future translation.

articles.title: HML-2 env knockdown by AAV9-mediated miRNAs attenuates amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-like manifestations in mice.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease, for which there is no cure. Although the precise aetiology of ALS remains elusive, growing evidence suggests a pathogenic role for human endogenous retrovirus-K (HERV-K) in ALS. Expression of HERV-K subtype HML-2 envelope protein in neurons causes neurotoxicity in vitro and induces ALS-like symptoms in mice. We investigated the use of adeno-associated virus-9 (AAV9)-mediated artificial microRNA (amiRNA) targeting the HML-2 env gene in an ALS mouse model. From an in vitro screen of amiRNAs targeting the HML-2 env gene, three were chosen and inserted in tandem into an AAV9 vector and validated in vitro. This approach provided robust silencing of the transgene, with tandem amiRNA achieving robust reduction in gene and protein expression levels. Its therapeutic effectiveness was tested in an HML-2 Env transgenic mouse model, in which the env gene is expressed under the neuron-specific thy1 promoter and develops an ALS-like phenotype. A single intracerebroventricular injection of AAV9 vector encoding the amiRNAs into the mice at postnatal Day 1 effectively reduced HML-2 Env expression in the brain and spinal cord at 84 days post-injection, which was the latest time point studied. Knockdown of HML-2 env decreased the loss of cortical and spinal motor neurons and alleviated muscle fibre degeneration and fibre-type grouping. This led to improved motor function. Our results provide compelling evidence supporting the use of multiple amiRNAs delivered in an AAV9 vector for treating forms of ALS linked to HML-2.

articles.title: Integrative spatial metallomics: a tutorial review of multimodal elemental imaging workflows, challenges and opportunities.
articles.abstract: Spatially resolved molecular assays are increasingly used to study human health and disease, revealing complex tissue organization beyond what is accessible through bulk analyses. While spatial transcriptomic, metabolomic, and proteomic approaches have rapidly matured, quantitative mapping of metals and trace elements in biological tissues and biominerals through elemental imaging remains comparatively nascent. Elemental distributions alone often provide limited biological interpretation without contextualization within the tissue microenvironment. Here, we summarize themes and computational strategies for integrating spatial elemental data with histopathology and complementary spatial molecular assays. We highlight multimodal approaches for tissue alignment, pixel-wise clustering, and correlative analysis, illustrated through limited use cases involving amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and kidney stone formation. In the ALS cohort, pixel-level elemental profiles were clustered and compared with annotated tissue structures. In the kidney stone cohort, spatial gradients and correlations in elemental and biomolecular features from the renal papilla through the medulla to cortex were examined. Finally, we discuss key challenges for cross-sample, cohort-level analyses, including differences in spatial resolution, normalization, tissue architecture, and mechanistic inference. Addressing these challenges will require interdisciplinary collaboration, enhanced biobanking practices, and development of computational and statistical frameworks.
articles.journal: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications

articles.title: Liposomal Delivery of a Riluzole-Butyric Acid Mutual Prodrug Enhances Neuroprotection and Cognitive Recovery in Experimental Alzheimer's Disease.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, impaired synaptic signaling, and persistent neuroinflammation. Current therapies primarily provide symptomatic relief and have limited effects on disease progression. Riluzole, approved for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, exhibits neuroprotective effects through modulation of glutamatergic signaling, but its poor oral bioavailability limits its therapeutic potential. Butyric acid, a short-chain fatty acid postbiotic produced by gut microbial fermentation, possesses well-established anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties. In this study, a mutual prodrug of riluzole and butyric acid was synthesized and encapsulated into liposomes to investigate its effects on drug distribution and preclinical efficacy. The prodrug-loaded liposomes exhibited an average particle size of 322 nm, zeta potential of -7.95 mV, and entrapment efficiency of 43.49%. Oral administration significantly improved cognitive performance and attenuated neuroinflammation and oxidative stress in an AlCl 3 -induced AD-like rat model. Administration of prodrug-loaded liposomes led to the highest concentrations of riluzole in brain homogenates among the relevant treatment groups. Overall, the prodrug-loaded liposomes demonstrated better therapeutic efficacy than the prodrug suspension, individual drug-loaded liposomes, and their respective conventional formulations. The enhanced therapeutic performance is attributed to the complementary pharmacological actions of riluzole and butyric acid, combined with the ability of the liposomal system to improve drug bioavailability and facilitate cerebral delivery.

articles.title: Protein Isoaspartate Repair in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: An Integrative Bioinformatic Analysis of the PCMT Gene Family.
articles.abstract: Protein homeostasis is a fundamental determinant of neuronal survival, and its disruption contributes to the pathogenesis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Protein L-isoaspartate O-methyltransferases (PCMTs) are evolutionarily conserved proteins involved in the recognition and processing of damaged proteins through the repair of isoaspartyl residues and protein quality-control pathways; however, their potential involvement in ALS remains largely unexplored. Here, we performed a comprehensive in silico characterization of the PCMT family (PCMT1, PCMTD1, and PCMTD2) by integrating structural, transcriptomic, single-cell, genetic, and protein modeling analyses. Domain analysis demonstrated that all three proteins share a conserved PCMT domain, while predicted S-adenosylmethionine-binding motifs were identified in PCMT1 and PCMTD2 but not PCMTD1, indicating evolutionary conservation with functional divergence. Expression profiling revealed that PCMT family genes are expressed in ALS-relevant tissues and broadly distributed across neuronal, glial, vascular, and immune cell populations in both healthy and ALS-associated brain single-cell data sets. Analysis of multiple independent ALS transcriptomic cohorts identified consistent upregulation of PCMT family members, with PCMTD1 exhibiting the most reproducible disease-associated expression changes across nervous system tissues and peripheral blood. Gene set correlation analyses further revealed distinct relationships between PCMT expression and neuronal pathways, with PCMT1 showing positive associations with axonal transport and synaptic signaling, whereas PCMTD1 and PCMTD2 displayed largely inverse correlation patterns. Rare missense variants identified in ALS patients were predicted to impair protein function and decrease protein stability, while structural modeling suggested that several substitutions may disrupt conserved residues and the local protein architecture. Collectively, these findings identify the PCMT family as previously underexplored candidates associated with ALS and provide a comprehensive framework for future mechanistic studies investigating their roles in neuronal protein homeostasis and neurodegeneration.

articles.title: The TNKS/PI31-proteasome axis as a central node in TDP-43 neuropathies.
articles.abstract: Pathological aggregation of Tar DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) and disruption of neuronal protein homeostasis are defining features of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and related TDP-43 proteinopathies. Efficient axonal transport of proteasomes is essential for maintaining local protein quality control in neurons. Proteasome inhibitor 31 (PI31) regulates both 26S proteasome assembly and dynein-mediated transport of 20S proteasomes. Although Tankyrase 1/2 (TNKS)-mediated ADP-ribosylation of PI31 promotes 26S proteasome assembly, its role in proteasome transport and its contribution to TDP-43 pathology remain unclear. Live-cell imaging was performed to examine 20S proteasome transport in primary cortical and motor neurons from wild-type and Prp-TDP-43 A315T transgenic mice. Protein interactions among TDP-43, TNKS, and PI31 were analyzed by immunoprecipitation and Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET). Insoluble protein accumulation and colocalization were assessed by RIPA/urea fractionation, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Proteasome assembly and activity were evaluated using native gel electrophoresis and a 20S proteasome-specific fluorogenic substrate. TDP-43 aggregation was examined by semi-denaturing detergent agarose gel electrophoresis (SDD-AGE). In cell models expressing TDP-43-FL, TDP-43-A315T, or TDP-25 and in Prp-TDP-43 A315T transgenic mice, pathological TDP-43 species formed distinct aggregates, ranging from oligomers to prominent cytoplasmic aggregates, yet all reduced proteasome activity, impaired axonal proteasome transport, and caused the accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins, PI31, 20S proteasomes, and TDP-43 in the proximal axon and cell body. Pathological TDP-43 sequestered TNKS and proteasome components into insoluble fractions, thereby limiting the availability of free and soluble TNKS for interaction with PI31 and subsequent PI31 ADP-ribosylation, ultimately impairing 19S/20S proteasome assembly. Notably, disruption of the TNKS-PI31 interaction or inhibition of TNKS activity recapitulated the proteasome dysfunction induced by pathological TDP-43, supporting a role for the aberrant TNKS-TDP-43 interaction and consequent impairment of TNKS-mediated PI31 ADP-ribosylation in TNKS/PI31/proteasome axis dysfunction. Pathological TDP-43 disrupts proteasome function by impairing the TNKS/PI31/proteasome axis, suggesting that this axis may represent a potential therapeutic target for TDP-43 proteinopathies. Selectively restoring this pathway may enhance pathological TDP-43 clearance while minimizing nonspecific proteasome activation, thereby providing a more precise and safer therapeutic strategy for ALS and FTLD.

articles.title: A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research.
articles.abstract: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

articles.title: Cancer versus Non-Cancer Patients Admitted to Hospice: a comparison study.
articles.abstract: Malignant disease remains the leading reason for hospice admission, and direct, patient-level comparisons of cancer and non-cancer patients within the same residential hospice are scarce. To compare sociodemographic and clinical characteristics, symptom burden, nutritional support, length of stay and outcome between oncological and non-oncological patients admitted to a single hospice. Prospective observational cohort study of 175 consecutive admissions over one year, after removal of duplicate records. Patients were classified as oncological (n=151, 86.3%) or non-oncological (n=24, 13.7%) based on structured case report form fields. Sociodemographic, functional (Karnofsky Performance Status, KPS), nutritional, symptom (Edmonton Symptom Assessment System, ESAS) and cognitive (Memorial Delirium Assessment Scale, MDAS) data were collected at admission (T0); ESAS completion was also examined at 1 week (T7). Categorical variables were compared with the chi-square or Fisher's exact test, continuous variables (reported as median and interquartile range, including ESAS and MDAS scores) with the Mann-Whitney U test; p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (q). Most non-oncological patients had a neurological disease (21/24), mainly neurodegenerative diseases, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and dementia. Non-oncological patients were older (median 78.5 vs 72 years, P=0.002, q=0.012) and had worse performance status at admission (median KPS 20 vs 30, P<0.001, q=0.006). Artificial nutrition was more frequent among non-oncological patients (37.5% vs 14.9%, P=0.018), although not after correction for multiple comparisons (q=0.060). MDAS scores were higher in non-oncological patients (median 13 vs 4, P=0.021). ESAS data were missing in about half of oncological and three quarters of non-oncological patients; no ESAS item differed between groups after correction for multiple comparisons, and the non-oncological group's valid ESAS sample fell to a single patient by T7. Length of stay (11 vs 8 days, P=0.518) and in-hospice mortality (80.0% vs 70.8%, P=0.455) did not differ significantly. In this single-centre series, non-oncological patients, mostly affected by neurological diseases, were admitted older, more functionally compromised and with higher MDAS scores than oncological patients, despite comparable length of stay and mortality. Apparent differences in symptom burden are confounded by substantial, likely informative, missing data and should be interpreted with caution. Whether these differences reflect later referral or the age profile of the underlying diseases cannot be determined from these data.
articles.journal: Journal of pain and symptom management

articles.title: Clinical Variability and Genotype Driven Outcomes in an International Cohort of 14 Pediatric FIG4 Patients.
articles.abstract: Biallelic FIG4 variants classically cause distinct conditions characterized by peripheral neuropathy (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4J) or skeletal dysplasia (Yunis-Varón syndrome). However, central nervous system involvement is increasingly recognized. The prevalence and specific characteristics of movement disorders within FIG4-related disease remain poorly characterized, prompting a need to redefine its clinical continuum. To delineate the phenotypic spectrum of FIG4-related disorders beyond established entities (Yunis-Varón syndrome, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4J, bilateral temporooccipital polymicrogyria, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis type 11) using an international multicentre cohort. We retrospectively analyzed clinical, genetic, and neurophysiological data from patients with biallelic FIG4 variants to redefine genotype-phenotype correlations, focusing on motor development, cognitive status, and movement disorders. Evaluating 14 pediatric FIG4 patients revealed a continuous phenotypic spectrum rather than the clinical entities previously described in the literature. Instead of the typical peripheral neuropathy classically associated with pathogenic FIG4 variants, the predominant clinical picture in this age group was a severe neurodevelopmental disorder. Patients showed profound motor and cognitive delay, with a subset additionally displaying distinct movement abnormalities such as dystonia and bradykinesia. Loss of functional FIG4 causes a broader and more severe disease spectrum with central nervous system involvement, including intellectual disability and movement abnormalities such as dystonia and bradykinesia. Recognizing these features should prompt clinicians to consider FIG4-associated disorders, allowing for optimized patient care and tailored therapeutic strategies.
articles.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

articles.title: Personalizing nutritional care in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS): a multi-perspective qualitative focus group study of experiences and challenges.
articles.abstract: Background : Proactive, timely nutritional care is important for people living with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (plwALS), as weight loss and malnutrition are associated with faster disease progression and shorter survival. However, previous studies have shown that there is considerable practice variation in nutritional care, and that care is not always delivered proactively. Objectives : To gain insight into how healthcare professionals (HCPs), plwALS and their primary caregiver experience nutritional care. Methods : A generic qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured focus group discussions. Five focus group discussions were organized: two with HCPs and three with plwALS and their primary caregivers. Data were transcribed verbatim and analyzed inductively using thematic analysis. Results : In total, 14 HCPs, 19 plwALS, and three primary caregivers participated. Analyses resulted in four major themes: (1) A gap between knowing and acting, (2) balancing providing and withholding care, (3) sufficiently informed to participate in shared decision-making? and (4) opportunities for improvement. Conclusion : Findings suggest that improving nutritional care in ALS requires clear and transparent communication to ensure that plwALS and caregivers are well-informed about the importance of nutrition and monitoring of nutritional status, and more involved in clinical decision-making. Clear explanations about the dietitian's role and nutritional care process may improve patient engagement and facilitate shared decision-making.

articles.title: Subtype and stage inference of tract-level diffusion abnormalities in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) shows substantial heterogeneity in clinical presentation and white matter involvement, but conventional diffusion tensor imaging analyses provide limited information on whether tract-level abnormalities follow distinct patient level patterns. This retrospective secondary analysis included 73 patients with ALS and 30 healthy controls. Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) from 11 predefined tracts were used as SuStaIn biomarkers, with healthy controls providing the normative reference for Z-score standardization. SuStaIn subtypes and stages were examined against Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R), King's stage, and peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD). The three-subtype model classified patients into cingulate callosal motor mixed subtype (n = 34), hippocampal cingulum posterior projection subtype (n = 32), and posterior callosal projection, MD predominant subtype (n = 7). Exploratory comparisons showed lower PSMD in subtype 0 than subtypes 1 and 2 (both p = 0.026), lower ALSFRS-R in subtype 2 than subtype 1 (p = 0.026), and higher SuStaIn stage in subtype 2 than subtype 0 (p = 0.025). Higher SuStaIn stage correlated with higher King's stage (rho = 0.318, p = 0.006) and lower ALSFRS-R (rho = - 0.289, p = 0.013). After adjustment, higher SuStaIn stage remained associated with lower ALSFRS-R (β = - 0.333, p = 0.013) and more advanced King's stage (odds ratio = 1.181, p < 0.001). Tract-level diffusion SuStaIn identified anatomically interpretable patterns of white matter involvement in ALS and provided patient-level stage estimates associated with clinical disease burden.

articles.title: Urinary Dysfunction in ALS Patients: Assessment With the Overactive Bladder Awareness Tool.
articles.abstract: To compare urinary symptom bother and overactive bladder screening positivity between patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and controls using the Overactive Bladder Awareness Tool (OAB-V8). This retrospective study included 101 patients with definite ALS and 324 controls. OAB-V8 scores were compared using Welch's t-test and multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex with HC3 robust standard errors. Screening positivity (OAB-V8 ≥ 8) was evaluated using Firth's logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Mean OAB-V8 scores were 14.0 ± 6.8 in ALS patients and 12.40 ± 5.10 in controls (unadjusted p = 0.026). The adjusted mean difference was 1.65 points (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.20-3.10; p = 0.026). Screening positivity was observed in 101/101 ALS patients (100%) and 272/324 controls (84.0%). The adjusted odds ratio was 41.03 (95% penalized profile-likelihood CI 5.75-5205.66; p < 0.001), indicating substantial uncertainty in its magnitude. ALS patients reported modestly greater urinary symptom burden than controls after adjustment for age and sex. These findings support clinical attention to urinary symptoms in ALS but do not establish their underlying urodynamic mechanism.

articles.title: Evidence of White Matter R 2 * Homogenization After Formalin Fixation.
articles.abstract: Disentangling intrinsic susceptibility-driven R 2 * characteristics in white matter (WM) from fixation-related effects using in vivo, postmortem (PM) in situ, and formalin-fixed PM ex situ MRI. DTI and multi-echo gradient-echo MRI were acquired in vivo, PM in situ and PM ex situ. PM cases included neurologically healthy individuals and patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Voxel-wise R 2 * values were obtained using a mono-exponential fit and evaluated both as whole WM averages and according to WM fiber-to-field orientation. For the PM ex situ orientation-dependency analysis, PM ex situ R 2 * data were registered to the corresponding in situ DTI acquisition. Averaged as well as orientation-dependent R 2 * profiles were pooled across WM and compared across conditions. Whole WM averaged and orientation-dependent R 2 * values differed across in vivo, PM in situ, and PM ex situ conditions. No differences were observed between PM in situ healthy and PM in situ ALS cases. Compared with in vivo measurements, both PM conditions showed elevated whole WM averaged R 2 * values and reduced orientation dependency, with the strongest R 2 * anisotropy in vivo and nearly absent orientation dependency in the PM ex situ condition. While orientation-dependent R 2 * is reduced but preserved in unfixed PM in situ tissue, it is largely eliminated after prolonged formalin fixation without rehydration, likely due to microstructural reorganization and protein cross-linking. Collectively, these findings indicate that orientation-dependent R 2 * measured in fixed tissue has limited translational validity, while underscoring its sensitivity to intact microstructural organization in vivo and in unfixed PM tissue.

articles.title: Pathological separation utility of plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) detected by a single-molecule immunoassay platform in neurodegenerative diseases.
articles.abstract: To establish age-stratified plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) reference intervals using a domestic Digital Single-Molecule Sensing (DiSMS) platform and to explore neuropathological profiles across amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), inflammatory demyelinating diseases (IDD) and healthy individuals. We enrolled 719 participants (510 healthy controls, 121 ALS, 88 IDD). Age-specific reference intervals defining the healthy boundary were established using the 2.5th-97.5th percentile method. Pathological separation utility was evaluated via age-stratified subgroup comparisons and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Plasma NfL levels in healthy individuals increased significantly with age (p<0.0001), with reference intervals of 2.68-17.09 pg/mL (20-49 years), 7.14-61.95 pg/mL (50-69 years) and 14.20-104.71 pg/mL (≥70 years). Out-of-boundary NfL elevation rates demonstrated prominent age-dependent fluctuations. In ALS, out-of-boundary elevation rates were 98.3% (57/58) for the 20-49 age group, 68.4% (39/57) for the 50-69 group and 50.0% (3/6) for the ≥70 group, capturing the aggressive tempo of primary motor neuron degeneration. In IDD-which primarily comprised patients in early, clinically stable phases-out-of-boundary rates were 17.0% (8/47) in the 20-49 group and 2.6% (1/38) in the 50-69 group. Age-stratified ROC analysis demonstrated exceptional separation capacity for ALS against healthy controls (area under the curve (AUC): 20-49 years=0.999; 50-69 years=0.964; ≥70 years=0.981) and against IDD (AUC: 20-49 years=0.910; 50-69 years=0.976). Intriguingly, in the 20-49 group where physiological ageing noise was minimal, the platform retained a modest capability to distinguish stable IDD from healthy controls (AUC=0.607). Age-stratified plasma NfL mapping provides a rigorous normative framework for defining population-specific healthy boundaries in China. Rather than functioning as a standalone differential classifier, the dramatic cross-sectional variance in peripheral NfL magnitude successfully maps the distinct pathological spaces separating primary, continuous neurodegeneration (ALS) from quiescent neuroinflammation (IDD) across the adult lifespan, validating the analytical utility of domestic DiSMS platforms.

articles.title: Anatomically Defined Motor Phenotypes Reveal Dissociated Trajectories of Progression, Neurofilament Profiles, and Survival in ALS.
articles.abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) may reflect structured disease trajectories. This study investigated whether anatomically defined motor phenotypes capture reproducible patterns associated with progression, serum neurofilament light chain (NfL), and survival. In a multicenter cohort of 1307 ALS patients, motor phenotypes were classified by region of onset, timing of propagation to a vertically distant body region (early ≤ 12 months vs. later), and the degree of upper (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) dysfunction. Intercenter consistency was assessed using the Friedman test and Kendall's W. Associations with ALS progression rate (ALSPR), NfL, and survival were analyzed using group comparisons and Cox regression models. Phenotype classification was consistent across centers (Kendall's W 0.75-0.89). Onset phenotypes were significantly associated with ALSPR, NfL, and survival (p < 0.001). Trunk onset showed the lowest log(NfL/ALSPR), indicating dissociation between rapid progression and relative NfL elevation. Early propagation was the strongest marker of disease aggressiveness, with higher ALSPR, elevated NfL, and reduced survival (HR 2.93, p < 0.001). In early propagation, NfL disproportionally increased with progression indicating a relative uncoupling of NfL from functional decline. Phenotypes with balanced UMN/LMN and predominant LMN involvement were associated with shorter survival (HR 2.51, p < 0.001). Anatomically defined motor phenotypes identify reproducible ALS trajectories with distinct clinical and neurofilament profiles. Early propagation provides an actionable risk marker of disease aggressiveness, while combined upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction or lower motor neuron predominance is prognostically unfavorable. These findings support integrating structured phenotyping into prognostic models and clinical trial stratification.

articles.title: Copper-Mediated Radiofluorination of the Excitatory Amino Acid Transporter 2 (EAAT2)-Targeted PET Tracer [ 18 F]RP-115: Alternate Synthetic Method.
articles.abstract: Excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2) is a key regulator of extracellular glutamate in the central nervous system. Dysregulated EAAT2 is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), highlighting EAAT2 as a potential target for PET imaging. We previously reported a multistep radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115, a CNS-permeable prodrug that undergoes esterase-mediated hydrolysis in the CNS to yield the active EAAT2-binding carboxylate. Motivated by recent advances in copper-mediated radiofluorination (CMRF), we sought to develop a more efficient late-stage radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115. A two-step radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115 using CMRF provided [ 18 F]RP-115 in high radiochemical yield (52.8% ± 2.1 %, decay-corrected from starting [ 18 F]fluoride ion, n = 4), high molar activity (355 ± 61 GBq/μmol), and high radiochemical purity (> 99%) with a total synthesis time of 70 min. Chiral HPLC analysis demonstrated that the configuration of the aspartic acid residue remained intact without racemization during both the CMRF and trifluoroacetic acid mediated deprotection. We developed an efficient radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115 via CMRF, achieving high radiochemical yield and molar activity. This efficient synthesis may serve as a basis for the future implementation of a CMRF-based automated radiosynthesis of [ 18 F]RP-115.

articles.title: Mitochondria-Associated Membranes as a Convergent Hub of Brain Aging: From Neurodegeneration to Cerebral Ischemia.
articles.abstract: Brain aging is the principal risk factor for both neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) and cerebral ischemic disorders, yet the subcellular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely defined. Mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs)-specialized contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria-sit at the intersection of two well-established hallmarks of aging, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis, making them an attractive mechanistic node for understanding age-related brain decline. In this review, we propose a MAM-centered framework that unifies neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathology under the broader paradigm of brain aging. We first summarize the molecular architecture of MAMs and their core functions in neuronal Ca 2+ transfer, mitochondrial dynamics, lipid metabolism, inflammasome assembly, and autophagic quality control, together with emerging evidence from non-neuronal brain cells. We then examine how MAM dysfunction intersects with five hallmarks of aging-mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation (inflammaging), and altered intercellular communication-drawing on evidence from physiological aging and cellular senescence models. Next, we discuss disease-specific roles of MAMs in cerebral ischemia and in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. A central theme emerges: Rather than a unidirectional decline of MAMs, brain aging is associated with a loss of MAM homeostasis, in which both insufficient and excessive ER-mitochondria coupling can be pathological and the shared deficit is the failure to maintain contact-site function within an optimal range. Finally, we consider age-relevant therapeutic and biomarker strategies targeting MAMs and their potential translation into geriatric neurology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate MAM biology across physiological brain aging, cerebral ischemia, and the four major NDDs within a single homeostatic framework, offering a unified perspective on the mechanisms of age-related brain decline.

articles.title: Neural stem cell-derived small extracellular vesicles ameliorate disease progression in the SOD1 G93A murine model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
articles.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that primarily affects motor neurons leading to muscle weakness, paralysis, and ultimately, respiratory failure. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) facilitate intercellular communication by mimicking the functions of their parent cells. In this study, we found that repeated administration of neural stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (NSC-derived EVs) improved motor performance and provided protection to lumbar motor neurons, the neuromuscular junctions, and muscle morphology in the SOD1 G93A transgenic mouse model of ALS. Furthermore, by analyzing the RNA-sequencing of muscle specimens from ALS-SOD1 patients, we demonstrated that the rescue effects of NSC-derived EVs might be linked to the p53 pathway. Compared to the PBS control treatment group, both TP53 and the p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis (PUMA) were downregulated in the spinal cord of mice treated with NSC-derived EVs. These data provide additional knowledge for the promising use of NSC-derived EVs as a potential therapy for ALS.
articles.journal: Journal of neuropathology and experimental neurology

articles.title: Neuroepigenetics of the Environmental Exposome: Molecular and Clinical Implications in Neurodegeneration.
articles.abstract: Neuroepigenetics studies the molecular mechanisms that regulate gene expression in the nervous system without altering the DNA sequence. The environmental exposome has emerged as a key factor influencing neuronal plasticity and brain homeostasis, contributing to vulnerability to neurodegeneration. This narrative review analyzes the role of neuroepigenetic reprogramming as a central mechanism linking chronic environmental exposures with neurodegenerative diseases. Evidence indicates that alterations in DNA methylation, histone remodeling, and microRNA regulation contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and chronic neuroinflammation. These mechanisms are critically involved in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Neuroepigenetics represents a central mechanistic axis in neurodegeneration by integrating environmental exposures with intrinsic biological processes. This framework offers new opportunities for the development of early biomarkers and targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: STMN2: Membrane-Binding Microtubule Regulator or Tubulin Effector?
articles.abstract: STMN2, a protein implicated in motor neuron degeneration, is widely viewed as a membrane-associated microtubule inhibitor, but emerging evidence challenges whether this activity defined its cellular function. Three alternative models integrates available evidence to offer perspectives beyond microtubule regulation. The vesicle cargo adaptor model proposes that STMN2 recruits diverse cargos to transport vesicles for axonal delivery. The membrane-bound signaling messenger model links STMN2 turnover to local signaling, effector, degradation, or effector release. The traffic director model proposes that STMN2 regulates cargo routing between delivery and degradative pathways. These models are not mutually exclusive and position tubulin binding as a regulator of STMN2 function rather than its defining activity.
articles.journal: BioEssays : news and reviews in molecular, cellular and developmental biology
